title: “FLEE SEXUAL IMMORALITY”: WHY PAUL SAID RUN INSTEAD OF NEGOTIATE
paragraphs: “FLEE SEXUAL IMMORALITY”: WHY PAUL SAID RUN INSTEAD OF NEGOTIATE

The temptation you keep trying to manage may be the very thing God is telling you to escape—and what waits on the other side of obedience is not merely a cleaner record, but a heart learning again that it belongs to Jesus.
There is a moment in temptation when you already know.
Before you tell yourself, We’re only talking.
Before you reopen the conversation you deleted last night.
Before you close the bedroom door.
Before you convince yourself that pornography is harmless because nobody else is physically in the room.
Before you start explaining to yourself why this relationship is somehow different from what Scripture plainly says.
Something inside you is already sounding the alarm.
And perhaps that is exactly why these words from Paul feel so startlingly severe:
Not discover how close you can get without technically crossing the line.
Not prove how spiritually mature you are by standing beside the fire.
The original Greek is even harder to soften:

The verb φεύγετε — pheugete carries the sense of fleeing, escaping, getting away. Paul does not present sexual temptation as a debate Christians should become skilled enough to win while remaining comfortably inside the room. His command demands movement.
Because Paul understands something about sexual sin that modern culture desperately wants us to forget.
That is where Paul's argument actually goes.
Read the command in its context rather than isolating it:
Then only a few lines later:
“For ye are bought with a price.” — 1 Corinthians 6:20, KJV
There is the Gospel underneath the command.
Paul does not simply say, “Run because sex is dirty.”

God created human beings male and female. Marriage and the one-flesh union did not originate in pornography, Hollywood, hookup culture, or human invention. Scripture places the one-flesh reality within God's design for marriage.
The problem is not that God hates sexuality.
The problem is that sin takes God's gifts and tries to enjoy them while removing God's authority.
And Paul tells believers to flee because something infinitely greater than temporary gratification is at stake.
Not promises that you will “do better next time.”
Suddenly sexual holiness is not merely about avoiding scandal.
Your body belongs to the One who was crucified for you.
Your phone belongs under the lordship of Jesus.
Your private messages belong under the lordship of Jesus.
Your hotel room belongs under the lordship of Jesus.
Your dating relationship belongs under the lordship of Jesus.
Your loneliness belongs in the hands of Jesus.
Even the parts of your life nobody else sees belong to Jesus.

Paul says immediately before his command that believers' bodies are members of Christ, and immediately afterward he describes the believer's body as a temple of the Holy Spirit. His conclusion is breathtaking:
“δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν.”
The question is no longer merely:
“How far can I go before this becomes sin?”
“How can Christ be glorified in my body?”
And sometimes the most God-glorifying thing your feet can do...
Joseph understood that centuries before Paul wrote to Corinth.
Potiphar's wife repeatedly tried to seduce him.
He understood that yielding would not merely violate his master's trust. He called it wickedness and sin against God.
But then came the day when discussion was over.
There was no accountability partner standing beside him.
No church congregation looking through the window.
Genesis says Joseph left his garment in her hand and fled out of the house.
Then, because of her false accusation, he lost his freedom.
But he did not surrender his faithfulness to God.
There are moments when running will make you look foolish to people who do not understand what you are protecting.
Tell a mature believer what has been happening.
Stop taking your phone into the place where you repeatedly fall.
Stop calling secrecy “privacy” when secrecy is feeding your bondage.
You do not have to demonstrate spiritual strength by remaining unnecessarily close to temptation.
Sometimes worship looks like shutting the laptop.
Sometimes spiritual warfare looks surprisingly ordinary:
Paul later gives Timothy remarkably similar counsel:
“Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace...” — 2 Timothy 2:22, KJV.
Notice what biblical fleeing is not.
It is not simply running from something.
Pursue these things with others who call on the Lord from a pure heart.
That last part matters more than many Christians realize.
You were never meant to fight every battle alone.
Conversations nobody is allowed to read.
Rooms where nobody asks what happened.
But the Gospel says something radically different.
Not because sin does not matter...
but precisely because Jesus is greater than your sin.
Maybe that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Maybe you are reading this after failing again.
You promised God last time was the last time.
Maybe you even felt clean for several weeks.
And suddenly the old doorway appeared again.
You cannot understand why God would still want you.
The Gospel is not permission to keep sinning.
Grace is not God pretending sexual immorality does not matter.
Jesus did not endure the cross so that we could become comfortable with the sins from which He came to save us.
But neither is the Gospel the announcement that sexually broken people are beyond redemption.
Look at the Christians to whom Paul was writing.
Immediately before this discussion, Paul lists patterns of unrighteousness, including sexual sins, and then says something astonishing:
“But ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus...” — 1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV.
That might be one of the most beautiful words a sexually broken person could ever hear.
Your sin may explain part of your story.
It does not have to own the ending.
Your pornography addiction does not get the final word.
Your adultery does not get the final word.
Your secret messages do not get the final word.
Your sexual past does not get the final word.
Your shame does not get the final word.
This is why repentance is so much more beautiful than religious shame.
The Gospel says Christ receives sinners who come to Him.
The Gospel says you need Jesus because you cannot cleanse yourself.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible after sin.
It agrees with God about sin, abandons the attempt to justify it, and turns toward Christ in faith.
And that means some readers cannot finish this article merely feeling inspired.
Perhaps there is a person you need to stop contacting.
Perhaps there is an app you need to remove.
Perhaps there is an affair you need to end.
Perhaps pornography has been discipling your imagination longer than Scripture has.
Perhaps you have been calling something “love” that requires disobedience to God in order to survive.
And perhaps the sentence frightening you most is:
Seek mature pastoral help and wise accountability. If another person is being exploited, coerced, abused, or placed in danger, getting appropriate professional or legal help may also be necessary.
Do not protect darkness merely because exposure is uncomfortable.
Your soul is worth more than your image.
And if you are married and your sexual sin has wounded your spouse, repentance cannot mean demanding immediate trust simply because you apologized.
Forgiveness and rebuilding trust are not identical.
And then repentance looks toward Jesus.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of humans becoming disciplined enough to rescue themselves.
It is the story of a Savior rescuing sinners.
Christ was tempted, yet without sin.
Christ went willingly toward the cross.
And the same Jesus who commands holiness also offers mercy to repentant sinners.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Not grace that calls darkness light.
Not grace that leaves chains untouched.
Grace that finds someone on the bathroom floor whispering, “God, I did it again,” and calls them out of hiding.
Grace that tells the adulterer to repent.
Grace that tells the pornography addict there is a battle worth fighting.
Grace that tells the sexually compromised Christian, “Do not make peace with what Christ died to free you from.”
Grace that does not merely cover yesterday...
but teaches us to walk differently tomorrow.
Maybe you have been waiting for the temptation to disappear before you become serious about holiness.
Paul never promised Timothy that youthful passions would politely vanish.
There will be nights when obedience feels expensive.
There will be moments when your body wants what your spirit knows you should refuse.
There will be times when nobody would discover what you did.
And in those moments, holiness becomes worship.
Not because resisting temptation earns salvation.
But because the person purchased by Christ begins to understand:
Some of you were this—and you were washed.
“Become pure enough for Jesus to purchase you.”
You were bought with a price; therefore glorify God in your body.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years trying to reverse that order.
If I can stay clean long enough, maybe Jesus will love me again.
You fight from the reality of His grace, not toward the possibility of earning it.
You confess because Christ is merciful.
You flee because Christ is worthy.
You pursue holiness because you belong to Him.
And when you fall, you do not build a house in the mud.
You learn where the trap was.
No more negotiating with the thing trying to enslave you.
No more asking temptation what terms it will accept.
No more standing beside the doorway pretending you are strong enough.
And if this exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not need to describe your private sin publicly. But you can take one small step out of isolation.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to know that failure does not have to be the final chapter.
Send it privately to the believer who has been drifting.

Not every act of sharing glorifies God merely because Christian content is involved. But when you sincerely spread biblical truth because you want Christ known, believers strengthened, and struggling people called toward repentance and grace, even something as ordinary as sharing a message can become an act offered to God's glory.
Following keeps these messages near you.
Saving keeps truth available when the battle returns.
Commenting reminds struggling believers that they are not fighting alone.
Tagging puts truth in front of someone you personally care about.
Sharing carries the message beyond the people we could ever reach ourselves.
But before you leave this article...
Paul did not say run because there is no hope for you.
He told you to run because you belong to Someone worth running for.
You were bought with a price.
You are not fighting for permission to approach the cross.
You are running from the chains because the crucified and risen Christ has called you His.
when loneliness starts rewriting your convictions...
when your flesh says, Just once...
when secrecy says, Nobody will ever know...
Run toward the Savior whose scars prove that your soul was worth pursuing.
